title: Asia stocks roar back as Taiwan jumps 6%, Nvidia probe rattles AI trade
full_text:
Investing.com -- Asian stocks rallied on Monday, following a recovery on Wall Street, although concerns over an investigation involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang tempered gains as investors reassessed the outlook for the artificial intelligence trade.
The MSCI Asia Pacific index climbed 2.3%, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 advancing 3.5% and South Korea’s KOSPI rising 1.6%. Taiwan’s Taiex jumped as much as 6.4%, its biggest advance since July, while the TOPIX gained 3.4%. The rebound followed a turbulent week in which Japanese and Taiwanese equities entered bear-market territory and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both lost more than 16%.
A gauge of U.S. semiconductor stocks rose 4.2% late last week as investors bought beaten-down shares amid easing concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress would impose tighter restrictions on the AI industry following the party’s sweeping midterm victories. The S&P 500 nevertheless recorded its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 lost $2.3 trillion in market value on Thursday alone.
Nvidia futures initially fell as much as 1% after the company's board announced an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. Huang had acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, while the board said it had no reason to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised.
Nasdaq 100 futures were last up 0.7% and S&P 500 futures had gained 0.6%.
Taiwan leads rebound as authorities move to stabilise markets
Taiwan’s Taiex recovered from a seven-session losing streak, its longest since 2022, after the market regulator and finance ministry announced measures to restore investor confidence.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and MediaTek each climbed at least 6%, leading the rebound after the technology-heavy market entered bear territory last week.
The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the permitted volume of intraday short-selling orders using borrowed securities to 3% of a stock’s average daily trading volume over the previous 30 sessions, from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short-selling to 130% from 90%.
Authorities said the NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) national stock stabilisation fund remained available for deployment.
Meanwhile, Brent crude fell 0.9% to $97.44 a barrel as U.S. President Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran were unlikely if negotiations over its nuclear programme made progress.
Investors were also awaiting U.S. inflation data on Tuesday for clues on the interest-rate outlook, with markets pricing in nearly an 80% probability of a Federal Reserve rate increase by year-end.
China, India and regional markets show mixed performance
Chinese and Indian equities also attracted renewed demand as investors rotated away from AI-exposed markets. Mainland China’s CSI 300 rose 0.3% and the Shanghai Composite gained 0.5%, while India’s Nifty 50 fell 0.2%.
China's October inflation figures offered a mixed signal. Higher energy and commodity costs lifted factory-gate prices, but weak domestic demand meant many manufacturers struggled to pass those increases on to customers, squeezing margins.
Elsewhere, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.2%, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 and New Zealand’s NZX 50 slipped 0.2%, respectively, and Singapore’s Straits Times Index was unchanged. Indonesia’s Jakarta Composite gained 0.8%, while Malaysia’s KLCI fell 1.2%.
The Philippines’ PSEi Composite dropped 0.7% as the country’s economy expanded just 2.1% year-on-year in the third quarter, slowing from 2.4% in the second quarter and 4% in the same period last year.
ANZ Group Holdings shares fell 4.5% to A$38.62 despite the Australian lender reporting full-year cash profit of A$7.59 billion, narrowly exceeding analyst expectations. The bank also increased provisions amid a more volatile economic environment.
The latest rebound offers some relief after last week's sharp technology-led losses, but investors remain cautious about AI valuations, regulatory risks and the scale of infrastructure spending. Attention now turns to U.S. inflation data and further evidence of whether the technology sector can sustain its growth.

title: Trump calls Nvidia’s Huang ‘honorable,’ says yet to discuss China allegations
full_text:
Investing.com-- U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday evening praised Nvidia’s Jensen Huang for his contributions to the country, and said he had not spoken to the CEO regarding allegations of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
“He’s a fine person… I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump told reporters at Palm Beach, Florida, on Sunday evening, adding that Huang has “done an amazing job for the country.”
“I have not spoken to him about it,” Trump said.
Nvidia said earlier in the day it was investigating a Financial Times report alleging that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Huang, in an internal note to Nvidia employees, admitted to the affair, and said he would fully cooperate with the board in its investigation.
The Nvidia CEO developed a close relationship with Trump over the past two years, with the president championing Huang for Nvidia’s progress in the artificial intelligence industry.
Huang has consistently accompanied Trump on his state visits, most notably China earlier this year and the UK in 2025.
Trump, when questioned over whether he would take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week, said “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

title: China CPI inflation misses forecasts in Oct; factory-gate prices accelerate
full_text:
Investing.com-- China’s consumer inflation slowed more than expected in October, while producer price inflation accelerated to its strongest pace in more than four years, highlighting the divergence between subdued domestic demand and rising industrial costs.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.7% year on year, below economists’ expectations of 0.8% and September’s 0.9% increase, data showed on Monday.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices were unchanged, compared with a 0.2% increase in September.
Get premium insights on key economic indicators with InvestingPro -- at 55% off now
In contrast, the producer price index (PPI) climbed 5.7% from a year earlier, accelerating from September’s 5.0% rise and exceeding forecasts for a 5.3% increase. The reading was the highest since June 2022.
China’s producer inflation has been supported by higher oil prices amid Middle East tensions, as well as demand from emerging industries such as artificial intelligence.
"Prices in other consumer-goods categories were still falling, suggesting that weak domestic demand continued to weigh on underlying price pressures," Capital Economics analysts said in a note.
Analysts expect the external price shock to persist over the coming months but fade next year, with producer prices returning to deflation and consumer inflation averaging just 0.4% in 2027.
The contrasting inflation trends could complicate Beijing’s efforts to revive domestic consumption while supporting industrial activity. Policymakers have rolled out measures to boost spending and address excessive competition, but a sustained recovery in consumer prices remains elusive.
Investors will now look to China’s October trade figures later this week for further clues on the health of the world’s second-largest economy.

title: Oil prices pare losses as Hormuz, Houthi tensions persist
full_text:
Investing.com-- Oil prices pared early losses on Monday and rose slightly after Iranian media reported that no ships had transited Hormuz on Sunday.
Continued hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis also kept oil’s risk premium in play.
Brent oil futures for January rose slightly to $98.35 a barrel by 23:24 ET (04:24 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 0.3% to $90.83 a barrel.
Crude had initially fallen after U.S. President Donald Trump said it was "highly unlikely" he will need to order more attacks on Iran.
Oil also saw some bargain buying after an over 16% drop last week, as a Democrat sweep of both chambers of U.S. Congress spurred increased bets that lawmakers will pressure Trump into ending the Iran conflict.

But tensions in the Middle East persisted, with Iran stating over the weekend that navigational aid systems in southern Hormuz had been destroyed, halting traffic through "unauthorized" routes in Hormuz.
This was after reports said three oil tankers had caught fire in Hormuz over the weekend, with Iran also stating that a tanker had hit mines in Hormuz.
The development kept markets largely on guard over continued disruptions in Middle East supplies, despite the results of the U.S. midterm elections driving some hopes for de-escalation.
Trump, in a Sunday interview with CNN, said it was “highly unlikely” he will need to order more U.S. attacks on Iran, as long as there was progress in negotiations with Tehran.
Still, Trump’s comments also came as the U.S. began an operation to crack down on Iran’s trade of advanced weapons and sanctioned materials through its land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Washington and Tehran have been in a stalemate for nearly nine months, with heightened tensions between the two causing increased disruptions in crude supplied from the Middle East.
Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group also persisted, with the latter seen attempting to attack oil giant Aramco’s corporate office in Riyadh on Sunday.

title: Gold climbs above $4,120 as precious metals extend rebound
full_text:
Investing.com -- Gold prices rebounded above $4,100 an ounce on Monday after stronger-than-expected U.S. employment data triggered a pullback, with investors weighing the prospect of further Federal Reserve tightening following the U.S. midterm elections.
At 23:51 ET (04:51 GMT), spot gold rose 0.8% to $4,123.60 an ounce, while U.S. gold futures gained 0.9% to $4,132.26. Silver advanced 1.6% to $52.7890 an ounce, while platinum climbed 1.2% to $1,557.25. Spot palladium rose 2.4% to $1,048.14, while palladium futures gained 2.3% to $1,045.00. The U.S. dollar Index fell 0.1% to 102.14.
Gold fell 0.4% on Friday and traded around $4,070 an ounce after U.S. data showed employers added 165,000 jobs in October, beating every forecast, while the unemployment rate edged lower.
The stronger labour-market figures reinforced concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further to contain inflation. Separate data also showed consumer sentiment unexpectedly improved in early November to a three-month high, adding to evidence of economic resilience.
The metal had previously recovered above the $4,000 threshold following the midterm elections, as Treasury yields and oil prices retreated on expectations that incoming Democrats would push for an end to the Iran conflict.
Investors also anticipated that divided government would constrain further government spending and borrowing, helping ease concerns about the U.S. fiscal outlook. Despite the recovery, gold remains around 20% below its level before the U.S.-Iran conflict erupted in late February.
ANZ analysts described bullion as volatile last week amid an uncertain economic and political environment.
Gold had rallied strongly after the election as falling U.S. Treasury yields and crude prices improved the outlook for the metal, but Friday’s stronger payrolls figures reversed some of those gains by reviving expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases.
Fed officials will receive another employment report and a full set of inflation figures before their December policy meeting, when markets expect another rate increase amid persistently elevated energy prices.
Traders will now focus on Tuesday’s U.S. consumer price index report for further clues on inflation and the interest-rate outlook.

title: Taiwan shares rally 6% as short-sale curbs and NT$500 bln fund lift sentiment
full_text:
Investing.com -- Taiwan stocks rebounded sharply on Monday, ending a seven-session losing streak that had pushed the technology-heavy market into bear-market territory, as new restrictions on short selling and government support measures helped restore investor confidence.
The Taiwan Weighted Index rose 5.8% to 42,022.14, after advancing as much as 6.4% during the session. The intraday rally was its strongest since July 31.
The rebound followed a sharp reversal in technology shares after the previous week's rout. Taiwanese and Japanese equities had both entered bear-market territory, while South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix had each lost more than 16%.
Chinese and Indian stocks, meanwhile, attracted renewed interest as investors shifted away from markets with heavier exposure to AI-related shares.
Among the leading Taiwanese gainers, Mirle Auto, Parpro, Flexium and Aurotek each advanced 10%, while VIA Tech rose 9.2%. Losses persisted among several smaller stocks - Vizionfocus fell 10%, Sino Horizon dropped 9.9%, Prime Electronics Satellitics declined 8.8%, Lerain Tech lost 8.8% and ACES fell 7.3%.
Major Apple suppliers also participated in the rebound. Largan gained 9.9%, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing rose 6.1% and Foxconn climbed 4.6%.
The Financial Supervisory Commission introduced new measures effective Monday, cutting the cap on intraday sell orders for borrowed shares to 3% of a stock's average daily trading volume over the previous 30 trading days, from 30%. It also raised the minimum margin requirement for short selling to 130% from 90%.
Separately, Taiwan's National Financial Stabilization Fund, which has NT$500 billion ($15.2 billion) available, was authorized on Friday to intervene in the market as needed to reduce volatility. The move marks its 10th intervention since the fund was established in 2000.
Broader Asian market strength also supported sentiment despite a separate Nvidia-related development.
The chipmaker's board is investigating whether Chief Executive Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, following reports about his relationship with a former executive at a company under scrutiny by US authorities. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and said he would cooperate with the inquiry.

title: Asian stocks bounce as AI, Mideast jitters recede; dollar firm on Fed bets
full_text:
By Jiaxing Li
HONG KONG, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Asian markets and US equity futures had an upbeat start on Monday, edging into positive territory after a wild week when tech-heavy markets in Asia suffered some of their steepest falls in years over AI.
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 2% after sliding 4.6% last week. Japan’s Nikkei index added 3.5%, while Korean shares climbed 1.8%.
Taiwan’s benchmark rose more than 6% after notching up its steepest weekly drop in two decades last week, when fears about AI profitability and infrastructure demand sparked a rout following wins by Democrats at the US midterm elections.
US stock futures, the S&P 500 e-minis, were 0.6% higher on Monday. On Friday, Wall Street equities rallied to end a chaotic week after heavy AI-related selling, helping to calm some nerves.
Global stocks had already been under pressure in recent weeks with the AI trade crumbling amid rising interest rates, and the US midterm results deepened worries about increased regulation of AI and data centres. But analysts say some dip-buyers might be emerging in a week relatively light on data and events.
"The only fundamental this week that matters is price," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.
"You could easily see a lot of people going, ’You know what, now’s the time to buy — blood on the streets. It’s not as bad as everyone thinks,’" he said. "It will be driven by flow, and fundamentals will mean very little."
Earnings reports due this week from tech companies including CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco Systems are set to put the profitability of AI ambitions to the test amid the massive costs of the build-out.
Meanwhile, a company-led investigation by industry bellwether Nvidia into whether its CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign spying effort could also stoke volatility, analysts said.
Nvidia shares fell about 3.5% in after-hours trading on the Blue Ocean alternative trading system, while perpetual futures declined roughly 3%, according to Hyperliquid pricing.
Brent crude fell to $98.2 per barrel after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress.
Elsewhere, China’s factory-gate inflation accelerated to its fastest pace in more than four years while consumer inflation cooled in October, reflecting persistent cost pressures from higher oil prices despite weak domestic demand.
FED HIKE BETS BUILD
A blowout jobs report on Friday showed US employers added 165,000 jobs last month, more than twice economists’ expectations and bolstering the case for the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December. Markets will be watching a US CPI reading due on Tuesday for further clues on inflationary pressures.
Market expectations that the Fed will increase rates at least 25 basis points at its December meeting moved up to nearly 80% following the jobs report, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
Comments from officials also supported expectations for a rate hike, with New York Fed President John Williams saying US economic growth has remained remarkably resilient in the face of successive shocks but inflation is too high and it is essential to bring it back to 2%.
That helped the dollar notch up its biggest single-day gain in five months. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies of other major trading partners, last traded at 102.2.
The European single currency was little changed at $1.1148. The yen was 0.2% stronger at 158.215 per dollar.
In cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin added more than 1% to $74,934 while ether was steady at $2,140, crawling back from their lowest levels in over two months as investors fretted that a Democratic-controlled US Congress would toughen regulation on digital assets.

title: Citi sees Japanese stocks gaining into year-end
full_text:
Investing.com-- Citi said Japanese equities were likely to recover toward the end of 2026, arguing that a sharp sell-off on November 6 priced in a recession it did not expect.
The brokerage said current share prices could not be justified unless the global and Japanese economies entered clearly defined recessions, starting with a pullback in U.S. AI and data center investment.
Japanese stocks fell sharply in early-November, with the Nikkei 225down over 7% so far in the month. Investors grew concerned that the U.S. midterm elections would lead to tighter regulation of AI and data center spending.
Concerns over more interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan also weighed, after the central bank officially declared victory against deflation, opening up the door to more monetary tightening.
This saw the Japanese stock decline extend well beyond the tech sector, which Citi said pointed to expectations of a broad deterioration in the economy and corporate earnings.
Citi estimated that the earnings per share (EPS) implied by the November 6 close was roughly 20% below current consensus. That was equivalent to a decline of nearly 30% in overall Japanese EPS for fiscal 2027, it said.
Downward revisions of more than 20%, or declines of more than 30%, had been seen only during recessions, Citi said.
The market also implied a fall of more than 50% year-on-year in fiscal 2027 EPS for the tech sector, as measured by MSCI Japan IT. Citi called that pricing excessive.
Tech accounted for only about 23% of TOPIX, and Citi said it was difficult to see overall EPS falling by more than 30% even if tech earnings halved, provided other sectors held firm. It said the market was effectively pricing in sharp downgrades outside AI and semiconductor-related names, which it called a clear overreaction.
The market had priced in steep EPS cuts on several occasions, most recently during the 2025 tariff shock, Citi said. In those cases, consensus EPS tended to decline gradually while market-implied EPS improved sharply, and share prices rebounded.
Citi acknowledged that Japanese equities could remain highly volatile in the near term but maintained its main scenario of a market pick-up toward year-end.

title: Equity positioning suffered one of its sharpest weekly drops on record: DB
full_text:
Investing.com - Global equity positioning has plummeted to a massive underweight, registering one of the sharpest weekly declines on record as forced unwinding hammered the technology sector, according to a new research report from Deutsche Bank.
The firm’s consolidated measure of equity positioning plunged to the 20th percentile. Discretionary investors drove the retreat, with their positioning tumbling to the bottom 3% of its historical band, while systematic strategies rapidly slashed their exposure back to neutral.
The rapid exit signals extreme investor pessimism, with large-cap positioning now aligning with expectations of zero corporate earnings growth. Deutsche Bank strategists noted this sharply contradicts current market fundamentals, given the median S&P 500 company just posted nearly 15% earnings growth in the third quarter.
Technology stocks served as the epicenter of the rout, with sector positioning breaking below the broader market to hit lows unseen since "Liberation Day". Current positioning implies that tech earnings growth is turning negative, despite the sector posting a massive 53% aggregate growth rate in the third quarter.
While market chatter blamed the tech sell-off on the recent "blue sweep" in the U.S. mid-terms - sparking fears over bipartisan opposition to data center expansions - Deutsche Bank attributed the plunge primarily to a "forced positioning unwind".
Despite the grim sentiment, the bank remains aggressively bullish on the sector. Strategists reiterated an "overweight" rating on tech, arguing the recent collapse has created a highly favorable risk-reward setup and describing the market as a coiled spring.
Surprisingly, the massive positioning unwind coincided with aggressive capital allocations. Global equity funds absorbed $89.2 billion over the week, hitting a 20-week high.
This surge was dominated by emerging markets, which registered a record $45.1 billion influx. Chinese equities absorbed the bulk of the emerging market flows with $34.5 billion, followed by Taiwan with $8.6 billion. Even battered technology funds absorbed $14.5 billion, indicating strong dip-buying behavior amidst the widespread market chaos.

title: China extends suspensions of 24% tariff on US goods, port fees on US ships for two months
full_text:
BEIJING, Nov 9 (Reuters) - China on Monday extended the suspension of its additional tariff of 24% on US imports and the suspension of special port fees on US-linked ships for two months.
• The 24% additional tariff on US imports will continue to be suspended for two months from 1:01 p.m. (0501 GMT) on Tuesday, but a tariff of 10% will remain, its state council, or cabinet, said
• The suspension of special port fees on US-linked vessels will be extended until January 10, 2027, China’s transport ministry said in a statement
• China is also continuing to suspend a probe into shipping and shipbuilding supply chain security, the ministry said.
• After September’s Washington summit of their leaders, both sides proposed a $60-billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly $17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has yet to be finalised
• China is extending the tariff suspensions to implement the "outcomes and consensus reached at the Washington meeting between the heads of state of China and the United States", the council’s tariffs panel said in a statement
• China has "noted that the US side has repeatedly stated that it intends to use Section 301 tariffs to replace the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that have been held invalid by judicial rulings" it said
• China will "closely follow subsequent measures taken by the US side and will, as appropriate, adjust relevant tariff countermeasures in light of developments," it added
• Continued suspension of some additional tariffs on U.S. goods will help ensure a stable and predictable policy environment for ties and promote development of China–U.S. economic and trade relations, it said

WEST PALM BEACH, Nov 8 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Sunday said he was "only kidding" when he suggested UFC CEO Dana White could become his next White House press secretary, after a social media post a day earlier stirred speculation about recruiting his feisty ally and signaled a combative approach to dealing with Democrats as they prepare to take control of Congress.

Trump said White would visit him at the White House on Monday, but added that the meeting was planned for other reasons.
White, who has led the Ultimate Fighting Championship for more than two decades, has been a close Trump ally and helped mobilize support for his 2024 presidential campaign.
He has also appeared alongside Trump at several political events and helped bring UFC fights to the White House lawn this year.

title: Trump says he wants UFC chief Dana White for White House press secretary

WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he had asked mixed martial arts promoter Dana White to serve as White House press secretary and called on him to bring some fighters along as assistants "even though some are not from our country."
White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, is a "violent Fighter and Warrior," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump also asked for six current or former UFC titleholders to join White, including two athletes from Russia’s Dagestan region, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov; Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and "Kayla Harris," likely a reference to Kayla Harrison; and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian native who became a US citizen last year.
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote.
Speaking at a press conference on Saturday while in London after a boxing event, White said he would meet with Trump at the White House on Monday.
The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia’s tenure ended last month after less than a week. Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August.
White and Trump first worked together in the early 2000s, when Trump’s Taj Mahal casino hosted some UFC events. But they have become closer allies since the UFC chief publicly backed Trump’s presidential campaign in 2016.
Trump in recent years has attended several UFC events, and in June the White House hosted a night of UFC fights as part of celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of US independence.
The White House press office already has a former UFC spokesperson in White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung, who worked for White’s organization from 2013 to 2016.

title: Huang allegations, Berkshire earnings, AI regulations - What’s moving markets
full_text:
Investing.com -- Investors are heading into a busy week with U.S. inflation data and fresh corporate earnings likely to shape market sentiment, while developments at major companies and a potential shift in Washington’s approach to artificial intelligence add to the agenda. Berkshire Hathaway’s latest results highlighted the strength of its cash position despite weaker operating earnings, while Binance announced a finance leadership change days after a major cryptocurrency theft.
As of 0342 ET, U.S. S&P 500 Futures rose 0.35%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Futures fell 0.3%. Dow Jones Futures climbed 0.6%.
Here are five things to know before markets open:
1. Questions surround Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following unverified allegations
A claim circulating about Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has alleged that he admitted to an affair with a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of having links to China. The claim also alleges that Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation.
However, these allegations have not been independently established in the information provided. They should not be reported as fact without confirmation from credible sources, including Nvidia and the individuals concerned.
Any verified development involving Nvidia’s leadership could attract investor attention given the company’s central role in the global AI industry. However, investors should distinguish substantiated corporate disclosures from unverified personal allegations.
Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares opened 6% lower.
2. Binance finance chief departs after $6.3 billion crypto theft
Binance Chief Financial Officer Kaiser Ng is leaving the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange to pursue another venture, the company said on Saturday, days after hackers reportedly stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency in a major security breach.
Binance Co-CEO Yi He said Ng had decided to leave after more than five years at the company, adding that a transition plan had been in place for the past six months. Justin Yek, a former vice-president of finance at Airwallex, will take over as CFO.
The leadership change comes just over a week after Binance disclosed that hackers had carried out a sophisticated attack that began months earlier, compromising employees’ computers. The exchange said the breach, which unfolded on October 29, involved malware hidden in software downloads and fraudulent recruitment efforts targeting engineers.
The FBI has attributed the theft to a North Korean hacking group, an allegation Pyongyang has denied. Binance has said it will fully reimburse affected customers.
The timing of the CFO transition could intensify scrutiny of Binance’s financial controls and risk management, even though the company says the departure had been planned. The incident also highlights the cybersecurity risks facing cryptocurrency exchanges and the potential impact of major breaches on investor confidence.
3. Berkshire operating earnings fall as cash reserves hit record
Berkshire Hathaway reported a 5.8% decline in third-quarter operating earnings on Saturday, as weaker insurance results weighed on the conglomerate’s performance.
Operating profit fell to $12.7 billion from $13.48 billion a year earlier, according to a regulatory filing. The measure is closely watched because Warren Buffett considers it a better indicator of the company’s underlying performance than net income, which can be affected by unrealized gains and losses on investments.
Despite the decline in operating earnings, Berkshire’s cash holdings climbed to a record $377.4 billion. The conglomerate also stepped up its share repurchases, buying back approximately $9.6 billion of its own stock during the quarter.
Berkshire’s growing cash pile suggests the company is maintaining substantial financial flexibility, even as it increases buybacks. The combination of record liquidity and elevated equity valuations may also offer investors insight into how the conglomerate is approaching investment opportunities and capital allocation.
4. U.S. inflation data and technology earnings take centre stage
Investors will turn their attention to Tuesday’s U.S. consumer price index report, one of the most closely watched measures of inflation and an important input for expectations about the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate outlook.
The report could offer fresh clues on whether price pressures are easing or remaining persistent, potentially influencing Treasury yields, the dollar and expectations for future monetary policy.
The corporate earnings calendar will also feature several technology companies, with CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco Systems scheduled to report.
A hotter-than-expected inflation reading could reinforce expectations that interest rates will remain elevated for longer, potentially weighing on stocks, particularly growth-oriented technology shares. Meanwhile, earnings from companies exposed to cloud computing, semiconductors and networking could offer further insight into the strength of AI-related investment.
5. Democrats plan push for tougher AI and data-center rules
Democrats are preparing a series of legislative proposals targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of Congress in January, according to lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates.
The proposed measures would represent a shift from the Republican-led Congress, which has largely prioritised promoting AI development rather than imposing restrictions on the technology.
Democrats are considering bills to protect consumers from higher electricity costs linked to data-center demand, require independent testing of advanced AI systems and clarify when AI companies could be held liable for harm caused by their products.
However, the proposals could face significant obstacles while Republican President Donald Trump remains in the White House. Trump has repeatedly opposed calls for mandatory federal rules governing AI.
The proposals could increase regulatory uncertainty for AI developers and companies investing heavily in data-center infrastructure. Potential rules on electricity costs, safety testing and liability could also affect the economics of building and operating AI systems, making the policy debate an important risk for the sector.

title: NextDC pauses uncontracted projects after Australian data centre woes
full_text:
By Christine Chen
SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Australian data centre operator NextDC said on Monday it would stop work on all projects without customer contracts following a big setback on a facility in Melbourne, as two major rivals finalised buying an A$715 million ($492 million) stake in the company.
A suspension of work on its flagship M3 data centre expansion in Melbourne due to power delays and community backlash forced the company to cut its earnings forecasts last month, sending its share price tumbling 42%.
The decision to pause uncontracted projects after the Melbourne delay is another blow for NextDC, which had been touted as Australia’s most prolific data centre developer.
"The last couple of weeks (I) certainly didn’t expect to be in the position we’re in today having to deal with some delays," NextDC’s chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told the UBS Australasia conference.
"That’s unfortunately probably reflective of the global environment in relation to the engagement, social license, people’s feelings about artificial intelligence and data centres being the physical embodiment of that."
Scroggie said the M3 delay meant the top priority was to win community backing for that project and "anything that didn’t have a customer contract and a customer commitment that we absolutely have to deliver on is now no longer a priority."
He did not say how many projects would be paused. The company had 11 centres in development or in the planning stages, according to its 2026 annual report.
"That work can’t restart until we clearly communicate that we’ve solved this problem, that we’ve earned the trust of everybody that’s been supporting us, and then we will get back to work."
NextDC’s rivals Goodman Group and its New York-listed partner, Digital Realty, bought a 9.9% stake in the company last week following the share price plunge.
"When you have a challenge like we’ve had in the last couple of weeks, it’s not really any surprise to me that people ... look at that and say, now might be the time," Scroggie said.
Goodman and Digital Realty said they had no plans at the moment to launch a takeover offer, but reserved the right to do so. They said they would "look forward to a potential collaboration with the NextDC board and management on the ways and forms in which the parties may help to address the challenges facing the company".
Following their share raid, NextDC’s share price recovered the ground lost from the earnings writedown.
($1 = 1.4520 Australian dollars)

title: Take Five: Tech wreck and roll
full_text:
Nov 9 (Reuters) - Traders on the world’s financial markets go into the week hoping the storm engulfing tech stocks blows itself out and for no new escalation in the Iran war that sends oil prices surging again.
There are also key US and Chinese data, the UN’s COP climate summit gets underway in Turkey, horse trading begins over the next ECB chief and New Zealand is in limbo after an inconclusive weekend election.
Here’s all you need to know about the coming week in markets by Dhara Ranasinghe, Alun John and Simon Jessop in London, Lewis Krauskopf in New York and Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore.
1/ HOUSE OF P-AI-N
The Democrats’ US midterm win has been the latest hammer blow to the once-unstoppable Big Tech trade.
The Nasdaq’s 5.5% slump on Thursday was its biggest since the Liberation Day rout of April 2025 and wiped $2.5 trillion off that one index alone.
Worries had already been intensifying about the stratospheric cost of the AI buildout. Now, post-midterms, the prospect of tougher regulations that slow everything down is hurting just as much.
Democratic wins in Texas and Georgia reflected the voter backlash against the data centres that are at the heart of the AI boom, but are also ugly and loud and require huge amounts of energy and water.
Some sense a compromise might be struck since AI has become a key economic driver. But if the rout resumes next week, growth worries will likely mount and plenty will be wondering whether something somewhere in the financial system tied to it all might break.
2/KEEPING A CLOSE CPI
US data and the direction of oil prices over the week could determine whether the Federal Reserve hikes its interest rates one more time before the year is out.
Tuesday’s US consumer price index (CPI) — perhaps the most closely watched inflation measure — is expected to show a monthly rise of 0.3%, according to a Reuters poll, while Friday brings another key read on producer prices.
As it stands, traders are pricing in a more than 80% chance of a Fed hike at its December 8-9 meeting. That would take the federal funds rate — the primary driver of global borrowing costs — to 4.00%-4.25% and follow the Fed’s first rise in three years back in September.
Then there’s oil. Crude prices have dropped 18% since the Republicans’ hammering in the US midterms stoked bets that President Donald Trump may look to de-escalate the Iran war. Over the weekend, the US President downplayed the likelihood of fresh attacks - as long as peace talks progress.
3/WHO’S IT GOING TO EC-BE?
European economic growth has been surprisingly resilient this year in the face of sky-high energy prices and rising borrowing costs.
The coming week will provide another test with quarterly employment data due, as well as a more refined estimate of quarterly GDP. Last month’s preliminary flash Q3 reading showed 0.4% growth.
If confirmed, it will boost the mood at Monday’s gathering of euro zone finance ministers, where another top topic will be who replaces European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde when she leaves Frankfurt in February.
Nominations have now been finalised. The two candidates are former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the head of the Bank for International Settlements.
The EU hopes to appoint a new ECB president by its mid-December summit, so it will have to get a move on. Monday’s meeting could be busy.
4/COP SHOW
The UN’s COP31 climate summit kicks off in Turkey on Monday, with more than 80 world leaders expected to attend against the backdrop of worsening extreme weather events that have caused a slew of devastating disasters this year.
With the US not formally involved under climate-sceptic Donald Trump, his humbling in this week’s midterms will be a glimmer of hope for some, although efforts to build coalitions of the willing to phase out fossil fuels and halt deforestation will need to continue.
As the Middle East war keeps oil and gas prices high, host Turkey is also pushing nations to accelerate the shift to green power so that 35% of the world’s power comes from electricity by 2035, from around 23% now.
Overhanging everything, though, will be the thorny issue of money. With development aid getting slashed by many richer countries, vulnerable developing countries will once again be looking for more help to cope with climate change.
5/THRILLER IN MANILA
There will be a flurry of last-minute diplomacy in Manila next week as senior government officials start the final preparations on Friday for the following week’s ASEAN nations summit.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who is hosting the November 15-17 gathering, has said Chinese Premier Li Qiang will be there, while both President Trump and his Canadian sparring partner, Prime Minister Mark Carney, are expected to attend too.
Indonesia is also likely to come under pressure for its wildfires that blanketed much of the region in thick smog earlier this year, with Singapore already vowing to strengthen an agreement on transboundary haze.
Elsewhere in Asia, Chinese inflation data has just seen producer prices notch their fastest increase in nearly 4-1/2 years, trade figures are due on Tuesday, followed by lending data later in the week.
New Zealand, meanwhile, faces weeks of uncertainty after its weekend election produced no clear winner.
(Graphics by Vineet Sachdev; Compiled by Marc Jones; editing by Andrew Heavens and Toby Chopra)

title: GEA shares slip as strong order intake fails to lift guidance, margin mixed
full_text:
Investing.com -- Shares in GEA Group edged lower on Monday after the German food and pharma machinery maker reported a 20% jump in third-quarter orders that was largely driven by large contracts, but revenue and earnings missed forecasts and the company left its 2026 guidance unchanged.
Order intake rose to €1.65 billion from €1.37 billion a year earlier, above the average analyst forecast of 1.50 billion and the highest estimate of 1.53 billion. Organic order growth, which strips out currency and portfolio effects, was 19.5%.
Large orders totalled €294.8 million, versus €64.4 million a year earlier, with €191.7 million from Nutrition Plant Engineering and €103.1 million from Pharma & Food Applications.
They included an order for continuous tableting technology, an area where GEA expects average annual revenue growth of 15% to 20% through 2030. Order backlog was €3.72 billion, up 20%.
Revenue rose 7% to €1.46 billion, short of the €1.48 billion expected. Organic growth was 6.2%, against a forecast of 8.1%.
EBITDA before restructuring expenses rose 12.6% to €260.9 million, slightly below the €263.6 million forecast.
The margin on that measure was a quarterly record 17.9%, against 17.8% expected. Net profit rose 6.4% to €128.5 million, and earnings per share of €0.79 missed the €0.85 forecast.
GEA confirmed its 2026 outlook, raised in July, of organic revenue growth of 6% to 8% and an EBITDA margin before restructuring of 17% to 17.4%.
Analysts’ full-year forecasts of 7.9% growth and a 17.3% margin sit at the upper end of those ranges.
Citi said the large orders were well above its forecast of €120 million, while base orders were 2% to 3% softer than it expected.
Base orders still grew 3% to 4% organically from a year earlier, but fell 7% from the previous quarter against typical seasonal weakness of 5%.
“Mechanically a likely 2-3% Street 2027 EBITDA upgrade from the larger orders,” Citi said, but added that the stock had been strong into the results, margin performance was mixed and growth-led upgrades were in lower-margin divisions.
Citi’s EBITDA forecast was 3% above the reported figure, and its margin forecast was 18.2%.
Free cash flow was €134.7 million, up from €52.2 million. GEA had net liquidity of €115.2 million at Sept. 30, against net debt of €36.3 million a year earlier, and spent €54.1 million on share buybacks in the quarter.

title: Nvidia’s shares slide as chip giant probes CEO over spy claims
full_text:
By Heekyong Yang, Kyu-seok Shim and Tom Westbrook
SEOUL/SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia shares fell sharply on Monday after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.
The internal probe followed a media report that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia’s employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.
The investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang’s future given Nvidia’s status as the world’s most valuable chipmaker and the CEO’s role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.
The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.
The fallout from the probe extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang’s daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.
Nvidia’s shares tumbled more than 6% in Frankfurt trading, extending last week’s selloff and pushing the stock to fresh multi-month lows. At those levels, the chipmaker stood to lose about $270 billion from its closing price on Friday, according to LSEG Datastream.
"The market’s probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there’s a lot of conjecture as to the build-out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.
But Weston said he did not think Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI", would be replaced.
"If we genuinely thought he was going to step down ... the stock would be down — it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest,” he said.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.
Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.
ASIA PARTNERS UNAFFECTED
Shares in Nvidia’s key Asian chip suppliers TSMC, Samsung Electronics (KS:005930) and SK Hynix rebounded on Monday after last week’s selloff of AI-related stocks. TSMC shares jumped 6.5%, while those in Samsung and SK Hynix climbed 2.9% and 4.7%, respectively.
Some prominent figures weighed in on Huang’s admission. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented, "I agree", on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership".
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about the allegations, but called him a fine person. "I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job," he added.
When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."
The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings roughly a year ago and chose not to do anything with the information.
CANCELLED VISIT
Madison Huang had initially planned to visit South Korean AI startup Rebellions and hold a question-and-answer session with Kakao Mobility. Rebellions said the events were cancelled due to "unavoidable internal circumstances at Nvidia."
Nvidia AI Day Seoul, a two-day event expected to draw about 2,000 participants to discuss physical AI, agentic AI and infrastructure, will proceed as planned, according to South Korean media. Nvidia did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
Analysts said a prolonged investigation or internal review could potentially delay Nvidia’s investment decisions or product launches, with broader implications for the semiconductor industry.
Ryu Young-ho, a senior analyst at NH Investment & Securities, said Nvidia’s rivals, including Advanced Micro Devices, could attract greater attention in the short term, potentially putting Samsung, which has close business ties with AMD, in the spotlight.
Still, he said Nvidia’s products would be difficult to replace, limiting the potential impact, although shipments to China could face further delays depending on how the situation developed.
South Korea’s deputy science minister said on Monday the government expected no disruptions to contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units despite issues currently facing the company.

title: Oil falls as Trump signals restraint on Iran despite fresh shipping attacks
full_text:
By Enes Tunagur
LONDON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell on Monday after US President Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran, though attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz kept supply concerns in focus.
Brent crude dropped by $1.65, or 1.7%, to $96.67 a barrel by 0830 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate lost 96 cents, or 1%, to $89.87.
The Brent benchmark plunged 16% last week for its steepest weekly drop since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
’RELATIVELY OPTIMISTIC SCENARIO’
"The (oil) market appears to be pricing in a relatively optimistic scenario of de-escalation, even though a comprehensive agreement between Washington and Tehran has yet to materialise," said Sugandha Sachdeva, founder of New Delhi-based research firm SS WealthStreet.
"Unless there is a meaningful diplomatic breakthrough accompanied by a sustained normalisation of shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil prices are likely to retain a geopolitical risk premium, with near-term support seen at $93 a barrel for Brent."
Trump said on Sunday that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
He had hinted at renewing attacks on Iran after last week’s US midterm elections, but there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation. Iran has said it would respond by striking US and Israeli targets.
Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade, called Trump’s comments "more measured" but said the market is still waiting to see whether the midterms have produced a lasting shift in Trump’s approach to the conflict, or whether this is just another temporary change in tone.
Oil is headed for a glut again as recovering Middle Eastern oil flows, rising production from other countries and weak demand have pushed global supply above consumption, JPMorgan said in a report on Friday, estimating a surplus of 1.1 million barrels per day in September, widening to 1.4 million bpd in October.
Separately, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on Saudi Aramco’s offices in Riyadh on Sunday.
Elsewhere, Russia’s Kirishi oil refinery was set on fire after a Ukrainian drone attack on the region on Monday, Governor Alexander Drozdenko said.

title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to "move faster" on climate
full_text:
By Valerie Volcovici and Simon Jessop
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Leaders of the COP31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as rising temperatures and an increasing number of climate-driven disasters threaten lives and the global economy, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday.
The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of AI compete for their attention.
"The urgency of this moment must drive us forward," UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in prepared remarks for the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was "nowhere near fast enough."
A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already set to overshoot 1.5C of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.
This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Niño, a UN report showed on Monday. 2026 has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.
Turkey’s COP31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.
Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.
"We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs," Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said in prepared remarks.
But climate advocates have criticised the pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.
WAR AND TECH
The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.
The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.
US President Donald Trump’s administration — which is shunning climate talks for the second year running — has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions.
South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.
"A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case," said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.
At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.
Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.
"This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer," he said.
"But the solutions are clear," he added, saying renewable energy installations had saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.
The rapid rollout of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.
Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at COP31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of COP31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.
"Paris is working," he said, referring to the landmark 2015 deal to limit global warming. "But we must move faster."
